single_run.intro_content: In a Single Run you execute exactly one algorithm on exactly one log — the simplest setup to get started. This walkthrough highlights the key spots; ESC or Skip exits at any time.
single_run.algo_pick_content: On the left you find the available tools, grouped by category. Clicking an entry selects it.
single_run.algo_help_content: Next to every algorithm sits a ? icon. Clicking it opens a panel with a detailed explanation — what the algorithm does, how it works, when to use it.
single_run.logsource_content: Two sources for the log: 'Upload File' for your own XES or JSON files (recent uploads are listed below), or 'Use Sample' for the bundled example log.
single_run.params_content: Every tool has its own parameters with sensible defaults. The preset bar above lets you save and reuse configurations.
single_run.run_content: Once algorithm + log + parameters fit, run via Ctrl/Cmd+Enter or click. The result appears inline with stats, tables, plots and downloads. Past runs land in the jobs panel on the right.

onboarding.step0_p1: Find out which complexity measures of process models and event logs capture the same thing. Load or compute a table of measures, check whether it suits a factor analysis, and read off groups of related measures.
onboarding.step0_p2: This quick tour shows the four things you'll use most.
onboarding.step1_p1: Model complexity analyses measures of Petri nets discovered from event logs, computed with ComFy. Log complexity analyses measures of the event logs themselves, computed with feeed.
onboarding.step1_p2: Both tabs work the same way.
onboarding.step2_title: Step by step, top to bottom
onboarding.step2_p1: Data, dataset, suitability, factors, loadings. Every change to a setting re-runs the analysis right away, and the loadings can be exported as CSV or LaTeX. An optional sixth step lets Claude propose names for the factors.
onboarding.step2_p2: The ? next to a heading explains the statistic; the Tour button walks you through the page.
onboarding.step3_api: API: drive everything from Python or curl; see the API page in the header.
onboarding.step3_history: Runs: every job of your session, including dataset computations.
onboarding.step3_inspect: Inspect a single log: run ComFy on one log and look at the discovered models.

factor.intro: Five steps from raw measures to factors, and an optional interpretation. Each step explains its numbers; the ? buttons next to a heading say more. ESC or Skip ends the tour at any time.
factor.data: Start here: pick a bundled dataset, upload a CSV, or compute the measures from your own files. Large computations run as background jobs.
factor.dataset: Check the size of the matrix and what the cleaning removed. You can download the cleaned data as CSV.
factor.suitability: Bartlett and KMO tell you whether a factor analysis makes sense at all. Exclude measures with low MSA here, by hand or with the filter.
factor.factors: The scree plot suggests how many factors to keep. Change the number or the rotation; everything below updates right away.
factor.loadings: The heatmap shows which measures load on which factor; bold values reach the threshold. Export the table as CSV or LaTeX for your paper.
factor.interpretation: Optional: Claude proposes a name and a short reading for each factor. Only the measure names, their definitions and aggregated results are sent, and every request costs money, so it runs only when you press the button. Always check it against the loadings.

help.cleaning: Before the analysis, rows where most values are missing are dropped. Then columns that are not numeric, that have no variance, that have missing values, or that are perfect copies of an earlier column are removed, as in ComFy for log measures. Such columns would distort or break the correlation matrix.
help.bartlett: Bartlett's test checks the null hypothesis that the correlation matrix is an identity matrix, i.e. that the measures are uncorrelated. If p < α, there are correlations that common factors can explain. With many observations the test almost always passes, so read it together with KMO.
help.kmo: The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin criterion compares the correlations between the measures with their partial correlations. Values near 1 mean the measures share common variance; values near 0 mean the correlations are mostly pairwise. Kaiser's scale: from 0.9 marvellous, 0.8 meritorious, 0.7 middling, 0.6 mediocre, 0.5 miserable, below that unacceptable.
help.msa: The measure of sampling adequacy (MSA) is the KMO value of a single measure. A measure with low MSA shares little with the others and fits no common factor well; removing it usually raises the overall KMO. Tick a measure to exclude it by hand.
help.msa_filter: As in ComFy, all measures below the threshold are removed and the MSA values are recomputed, until every remaining measure reaches the threshold.
help.scree: The scree plot shows the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix in descending order. Look for the elbow where the curve flattens; factors after it add little. The elbow and the eigenvalue-above-1 rule can disagree, so treat both as starting points.
help.eigenvalue: An eigenvalue is the variance a factor explains, in units of one standardised measure. The suggestion keeps every factor with an eigenvalue above 1 (Kaiser criterion), i.e. every factor that explains more than a single measure.
help.rotation: Rotation turns the factor solution so that each measure loads strongly on as few factors as possible, which makes the factors easier to name. It does not change how much variance the factors explain together. Varimax and quartimax keep the factors uncorrelated; promax and oblimin let them correlate, which is often more realistic for complexity measures.
help.threshold: Loadings with an absolute value at or above this threshold count as substantial. Each measure is assigned to the factor where its absolute loading is highest, if that loading reaches the threshold. Common choices lie between 0.3 and 0.5; ComFy uses 0.35, ComFy for log measures 0.5.
help.loading: A loading says how strongly a measure goes along with a factor. For orthogonal rotations it is the correlation between measure and factor. For oblique rotations the pattern matrix holds regression weights and the structure matrix the correlations. The sign gives the direction: measures with opposite signs on the same factor move in opposite directions.
help.communality: The communality h² is the share of a measure's variance that all kept factors explain together. A low value (below about 0.4) means the factors do not capture the measure well.
help.variance: SS loadings is the sum of squared loadings of a factor. Divided by the number of measures it gives the proportion of the total variance the factor explains; the cumulative row adds these up.
help.groups: Each factor with the measures assigned to it, strongest loading first. Measures in one group capture a similar aspect of complexity; the name of the factor is up to your interpretation.
help.communality_threshold: Measures whose communality is below this value are left unassigned, because the factors explain too little of them. ComFy for log measures uses 0.5; 0 keeps every measure.
help.factor_correlations: With an oblique rotation the factors may correlate. Values near 0 mean the factors are nearly independent; large values mean they measure related aspects.

warnings.bartlett_not_significant: Bartlett's test is not significant (p = {p} ≥ {alpha}); the measures may be uncorrelated.
warnings.singular: The correlation matrix is singular; these measures are linearly dependent: {groups}. Results rely on clamped eigenvalues and pseudo-inverses; consider excluding one measure of each group.
warnings.kmo_low: The overall MSA {overall} is below {threshold}; a factor analysis is not recommended.
warnings.small_sample: {n} observations for {measures} measures; at least 5 per measure ({recommended}) are recommended.
warnings.not_identified: {factors} factors for {measures} measures exceed the Ledermann bound; the solution is not identified and the loadings are not unique. Use fewer factors.
warnings.fit_not_converged: The factor fit did not converge: {message}
warnings.single_factor_no_rotation: No rotation is applied to a single factor.
warnings.heywood: Communality at the bound of the fit (uniqueness at most 0.005) for {measures}; possible Heywood case.

interpretation.intro: Claude reads the loadings together with the definitions of the measures and proposes a name and a short interpretation for each factor. Sent to Anthropic are the measure (column) names, their catalog definitions and aggregated results such as loadings and test statistics; measure values, row labels and file names are not sent. Each request costs money, so it runs only when you ask for it.
interpretation.running: Claude is interpreting the factors. This can take up to three minutes.
